correctness.rationale: For each fixed x>0 and even N→∞, differentiation of the superexponentially decaying Macdonald representation yields D_N(x)=∫_0^∞exp(N log t-x cosh t)dt. The phase is strictly concave with unique saddle xtsinh t=N, B=N/t²+xcosh t∼N/t. On the √B centered scale, the third and fourth standardized derivatives are O(B^-1/2) and O(B^-1); after Gaussian localization, odd terms integrate to zero and the fourth/squared-third terms yield Q_N=Phi_fourth/(8B²)+5(Phi_third)²/(24B³). Uniform local derivative bounds and strictly decaying tails justify O(B^-2)=O_x(t²/N²) as an integrated relative error. The saddle equation gives Phi_third/B→-1, Phi_fourth/B→-1, N/(Bt)→1 and (N/t)Q_N→-1/8+5/24=1/12. Independently centered quadratures for (x,N)=(1,60),(1,200),(3,600) gave scaled remainder roughly -0.0186,-0.0177,-0.0177 and verified the predicted order; these samples are not a limit proof. Not uniform in varying x; odd N derivatives at order zero vanish.

value.rationale: For the natural high-index order derivatives of a classical special function, the paper supplies an explicit, computable saddle normalization and sharp first non-Gaussian correction 1/12, with quantitative relative error O_x((log N)^2/N²). This improves asymptotic understanding of an object studied with numerical algorithms up to large derivative orders and separates it from generic large-Bessel-order or argument-derivative asymptotics. The standard Laplace technique itself is not claimed novel.
